The **University of Warwick** ([/ˈ w ɒr ɪ k/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_WORR-ik_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); abbreviated as _**Warw.**_ in [post-nominal letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-nominal_letters "Post-nominal letters")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-5)) is a [public research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_research_university "Public research university") on the outskirts of [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry") between the [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(county) "West Midlands (county)") and [Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwickshire "Warwickshire"), England.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-6) The university was founded in 1965 as part of a government initiative to expand higher education. [Warwick Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Business_School "Warwick Business School") was established in 1967, Warwick Law School in 1968, [Warwick Manufacturing Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMG,_University_of_Warwick "WMG, University of Warwick") (WMG) in 1980, and [Warwick Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Medical_School "Warwick Medical School") in 2000. Warwick incorporated [Coventry College of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_College_of_Education "Coventry College of Education") in 1979 and [Horticulture Research International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticulture_Research_International "Horticulture Research International") in 2004.

Warwick is primarily based on a 290-hectare (720-acre) campus on the outskirts of Coventry, with a satellite campus in [Wellesbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesbourne "Wellesbourne") and a central London base at [the Shard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shard "The Shard"). It is organised into three faculties—Arts; Science, Engineering and Medicine; and Social Sciences—within which there are thirty-two departments. [By the end of 2023, the student population was over 28,000 of which over 9,000 are postgraduates.](https://warwick.ac.uk/about/history/) The annual income of the institution for 2024–2025 was £859.9 million, of which £147.5 million was from research grants and contracts, with an expenditure of £828.7 million.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-annacc-1)[Warwick Arts Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Arts_Centre "Warwick Arts Centre") is a multi-venue arts complex in the university's main campus and is the largest venue of its kind in the UK outside of London.

In 2024, Warwick [ranked tenth nationally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_the_United_Kingdom "Rankings of universities in the United Kingdom") for [undergraduate education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_education "Undergraduate education"). Warwick is a member of [AACSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACSB "AACSB"), the [Association of Commonwealth Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Commonwealth_Universities "Association of Commonwealth Universities"), the [Association of MBAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_MBAs "Association of MBAs"), [EQUIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EQUIS "EQUIS"), the [European University Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_University_Association "European University Association"), the [Midlands Innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_Innovation "Midlands Innovation") group, the [Russell Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group"), [Sutton 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust "Sutton Trust") and [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK"). It is the only European member of the [Center for Urban Science and Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Urban_Science_and_Progress "Center for Urban Science and Progress"), a collaboration with [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University"). The university has extensive commercial activities, including the [University of Warwick Science Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick_Science_Park "University of Warwick Science Park") and [WMG, University of Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMG,_University_of_Warwick "WMG, University of Warwick").

Warwick's alumni and staff include winners of the [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize"), [Turing Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award"), [Fields Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_Medal "Fields Medal"), [Richard W. Hamming Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_Richard_W._Hamming_Medal "IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal"), [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award "Emmy Award"), [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award"), and the [Padma Vibhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Vibhushan "Padma Vibhushan"), and are fellows to the [British Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy"), the [Royal Society of Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Literature "Royal Society of Literature"), the [Royal Academy of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Engineering "Royal Academy of Engineering"), and the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society"). Alumni also include heads of state, government officials, leaders in intergovernmental organisations, and a former chief economist at the [Bank of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England "Bank of England"). Researchers at Warwick have also made significant contributions such as the development of [penicillin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penicillin "Penicillin"), [music therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_therapy "Music therapy"), the [Washington Consensus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Consensus "Washington Consensus"), computing standards, including [ISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization "International Organization for Standardization") and [ECMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECMAScript "ECMAScript"), [complexity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory "Computational complexity theory"), [contract theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_theory "Contract theory"), and the [International Political Economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_political_economy "International political economy") as a field of study. Warwick is also known for being the center of the experimental [cultural theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_theorist "Cultural theorist") collective [Cybernetic Culture Research Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybernetic_Culture_Research_Unit "Cybernetic Culture Research Unit"), which had significant influence on [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy"), [occultism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult"), and the [cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk "Cyberpunk") genre.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Twentieth century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Twentieth century")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Library_Under_Construction_1965.png/250px-Library_Under_Construction_1965.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Library_Under_Construction_1965.png)

Library under construction in the 1960s

The idea for a university in Warwickshire was first mooted shortly after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), although it was not founded for a further two decades. A partnership of the city and county councils ultimately provided the impetus for the university to be established on a 400-acre (1.6 km 2) site jointly granted by the two authorities.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-rees-7) There was some discussion between local sponsors from both the city and county over whether it should be named after Coventry or Warwickshire.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-rees-7) The name "University of Warwick" was adopted, even though [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick "Warwick"), the county town, lies some 8 miles (13 km) to its southwest and [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry")'s city centre is only 3.5 miles (5.6 km) northeast of the campus.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-11) The establishment of the University of Warwick was given approval by the government in 1961 and it received its [Royal Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Charter "Royal Charter") of Incorporation in 1965. Since then, the university has incorporated the former [Coventry College of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_College_of_Education "Coventry College of Education") in 1979 and has extended its land holdings by the continuing purchase of adjoining farm land. The university also benefited from a substantial donation from the family of John Martin, a Coventry businessman who had made a fortune from investment in [Smirnoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smirnoff "Smirnoff") vodka, and which enabled the construction of the [Warwick Arts Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Arts_Centre "Warwick Arts Centre").

The university admitted its first, small intake of graduate students in 1964, and took its first 450 undergraduates in October 1965. Since its establishment Warwick has expanded its grounds to 721 acres (2.9 km 2), with many modern buildings and academic facilities, lakes, and woodlands. In the 1960s and 1970s, Warwick had a reputation as a politically radical institution.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-12) Under Vice-Chancellor [Lord Butterworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Butterworth "Lord Butterworth"), Warwick was the first UK university to adopt a business approach to higher education, develop close links with the business community and exploit the commercial value of its research. These tendencies were discussed by British historian and then-Warwick lecturer, [E. P. Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._P._Thompson "E. P. Thompson"), in his 1970 edited book _Warwick University Ltd._.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-13) The Leicester Warwick Medical School, a new medical school based jointly at Warwick and Leicester University, opened in September 2000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-14)

On the recommendation of then-Prime Minister [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") chose Warwick as the venue for his last major foreign policy address as [US President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") in December 2000. [Sandy Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Berger "Sandy Berger"), Clinton's [National Security Advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Advisor_(United_States) "National Security Advisor (United States)"), explaining the decision in a press briefing on 7 December 2000, said that: "Warwick is one of Britain's newest and finest research universities, singled out by Prime Minister Blair as a model both of academic excellence and independence from the government."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:2-15)

### Twenty-first century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Twenty-first century")]

The university was seen as a favoured institution of the [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") government during the New Labour years from 1997 to 2010.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-recentquote-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:1-17) It was academic partner for a number of flagship Government schemes including the [National Academy for Gifted and Talented Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_for_Gifted_and_Talented_Youth "National Academy for Gifted and Talented Youth") and the [NHS University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHS_University "NHS University") which is now defunct. [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") described Warwick as "a beacon among British universities for its dynamism, quality and entrepreneurial zeal".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-recentquote-16) In a 2012 study by Virgin Media Business, Warwick was described as the most "digitally-savvy" UK university.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-virginmediabusiness.co.uk-18)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Maths_foyer%2C_Warwick_University.jpg/250px-Maths_foyer%2C_Warwick_University.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maths_foyer,_Warwick_University.jpg)

[Ian Davenport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Davenport_(artist) "Ian Davenport (artist)")'s _Everything_ (2004) in the Warwick Mathematics Institute[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-19)

In February 2001, [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") donated a new [S/390](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_System/390 "IBM System/390") computer and software worth £2 million to Warwick, to form part of a "Grid" enabling users to remotely share computing power.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-20) In April 2004 Warwick merged with the [Wellesbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesbourne "Wellesbourne") and [Kirton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirton,_Lincolnshire "Kirton, Lincolnshire") sites of [Horticulture Research International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticulture_Research_International "Horticulture Research International").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-21) In July 2004 Warwick was the location for an important agreement between the Labour Party and the trade unions on Labour policy and trade union law, which has subsequently become known as the "[Warwick Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Agreement "Warwick Agreement")".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-22)

In June 2006, the new [University Hospital Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Hospital_Coventry "University Hospital Coventry") opened, including a 102,000 sq ft (9,500 m 2) university clinical sciences building.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-23) Warwick Medical School was granted independent degree-awarding status in 2007, and the School's partnership with the University of Leicester was dissolved in the same year.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-medhist-25) In February 2010, [Lord Bhattacharyya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumar_Bhattacharyya,_Baron_Bhattacharyya "Kumar Bhattacharyya, Baron Bhattacharyya"), director and founder of the [WMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMG,_University_of_Warwick "WMG, University of Warwick") unit at Warwick, made a £1 million donation to the university to support science grants and awards.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-27)

In February 2012, Warwick and Melbourne-based [Monash University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monash_University "Monash University") announced the formation of a strategic partnership, including the creation of ten joint senior academic posts, new dual master's and joint doctoral degrees, and co-ordination of research programmes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-28) In March 2012, Warwick and [Queen Mary, University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Mary,_University_of_London "Queen Mary, University of London") announced the creation of a strategic partnership, including research collaboration, some joint teaching of English, history and computer science undergraduates, and the creation of eight joint post-doctoral research fellowships.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-30)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/WTC_Steve_Walton_IMG_9613WarwickArtsCentre_edit.jpg/250px-WTC_Steve_Walton_IMG_9613WarwickArtsCentre_edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WTC_Steve_Walton_IMG_9613WarwickArtsCentre_edit.jpg)

[Warwick Arts Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Arts_Centre "Warwick Arts Centre") (c. 2012), with White Koan (1971) by Liliane Lijn in the foreground

In April 2012, it was announced that Warwick would be the only European university participating in the Center for Urban Science and Progress, an applied science research institute to be based in New York consisting of an international consortium of universities and technology companies led by [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") and NYU-Poly.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-31) In August 2012, Warwick and five other Midlands-based universities—[Aston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_University "Aston University"), the [University of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham "University of Birmingham"), the [University of Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester"), [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") and the [University of Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham "University of Nottingham")—formed the M5 Group, a regional bloc intended to maximise the member institutions' research income and enable closer collaboration.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-32)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Prev_warwick_logo.png/250px-Prev_warwick_logo.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prev_warwick_logo.png)

Warwick logo before introduction of the current logo in 2015

In September 2013, it was announced that a new [National Automotive Innovation Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Automotive_Innovation_Campus "National Automotive Innovation Campus") would be built by [WMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMG,_University_of_Warwick "WMG, University of Warwick") at Warwick's main campus at a cost of £100 million, with £50 million to be contributed by [Jaguar Land Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_Land_Rover "Jaguar Land Rover") and £30 million by [Tata Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_Motors "Tata Motors").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-34) The centre will open in Summer 2018.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-35) The building was opened by [HRH The Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Prince_of_Wales "Charles, Prince of Wales") on 18 February 2020.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-37)

In July 2014, the government announced that Warwick would be the host for the £1 billion [Advanced Propulsion Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Propulsion_Centre "Advanced Propulsion Centre") (APC), a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization "Non-profit organization") that facilitates funding to UK-based research and development projects developing low-carbon emission powertrain technologies.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-38) The APC manages a £1 billion investment fund, which is jointly supplied by the [automotive industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry_in_the_United_Kingdom "Automotive industry in the United Kingdom") – via the [Automotive Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_Council_UK "Automotive Council UK") – and the [UK government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") through the [Department for Business and Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business_and_Trade "Department for Business and Trade") and managed by [Innovate UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innovate_UK "Innovate UK").

In September 2015, Warwick celebrated its 50th anniversary and was designated "[University of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_University_of_the_Year "Sunday Times University of the Year")" by _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ and _[The Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Times "The Sunday Times")_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-39) In December 2017, the university announced it would not continue with a project to open a Campus in [Roseville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseville,_California "Roseville, California").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-40) The university had spent £1.2 million on the project.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-41)

In 2023, the students' union voted for all the union-run catering to offer all plant-based meals. The vote was supported in order to reduce climate change emissions. According to plan, by the following academic year, the menus would be 50% vegan and then would be fully plant-based by 2027. It was the eighth student union at a U.K. university to adopt plant-based catering.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-42) Only 4,5% or 1,472 students out of 28,621 voted in ballot, among whom 772 voted in favour of plan. In 2024 this decision was revoked by students' union trustees due to "practical and financial challenges involved with such a significant transition".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-44)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Campus")]

Warwick is located on the outskirts of [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry"), 3.4 mi (5.5 km) southwest of the city centre and not in the town of [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick "Warwick") as its name suggests. The university's main site comprises three contiguous campuses, all within walking distance of each other. The university also owns a site in [Wellesbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesbourne "Wellesbourne"), acquired in 2004 when it merged with [Horticulture Research International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticulture_Research_International "Horticulture Research International").

### Main campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Main campus")]

The main Warwick campus occupies 710 acres (2.88 km 2) between the City of [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry") and the County of [Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwickshire "Warwickshire"). The original buildings of the campus are in contemporary 1960s architecture. The campus contains all of the main student amenities, all but four of the student halls of residence, and the Students' Union. The campus is split between the parliamentary constituencies of [Kenilworth and Southam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenilworth_and_Southam "Kenilworth and Southam") and [Coventry South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_South "Coventry South").

#### Warwick Arts Centre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Warwick Arts Centre")]

Main article: [Warwick Arts Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Arts_Centre "Warwick Arts Centre")

[![Image 13: The new front entrance for Warwick Arts Centre, with large screen.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Warwick_Arts_Centre%2C_University_of_Warwick%2C_Coventry_UK.jpg/250px-Warwick_Arts_Centre%2C_University_of_Warwick%2C_Coventry_UK.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Warwick_Arts_Centre,_University_of_Warwick,_Coventry_UK.jpg)

Warwick Arts Centre – main entrance (c.December 2022)

The [Warwick Arts Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Arts_Centre "Warwick Arts Centre") is a multi-venue arts complex situated at the centre of Warwick's main campus.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-45) It attracts around 300,000 visitors a year to over 3,000 individual events spanning contemporary and classical music, drama, dance, comedy, films and visual art. The centre comprises six principal spaces: the Butterworth Hall, a 1,500-seat concert hall; a 550-seat theatre; a 180-seat theatre studio; three cinema screens; the Mead Gallery, an art gallery; and the Music Centre, with practice rooms, and an ensemble rehearsal room where music societies and groups can rehearse. In addition the site includes a restaurant/ café.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Biology_Daily-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Warwick_Music_Centre-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-The_London_Korean_Film_Festival_2012-48)

#### University House

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: University House")]

In 2003, Warwick acquired the former headquarters of [National Grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Grid_plc "National Grid plc"), which it converted into an administration building renamed University House. There is a student-run facility called the ‘Learning Grid’ in the building, which includes two floors of PC clusters, scanners, photocopiers, a reference library, interactive whiteboards and plasma screens for use by individuals and for group work.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-49)

#### Koan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Koan")]

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a3/Helen_Martin_Arts_Studio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helen_Martin_Arts_Studio.jpg)

The _Koan_ in front of the Helen Martin Arts Studio

The _White Koan_ is a modern art sculpture by [Liliane Lijn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liliane_Lijn "Liliane Lijn") which is installed outside the back entrance to the Warwick Arts Centre.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Lijn-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-51) The _Koan_ is 6 metres (20 ft) high,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Lijn-50) white in colour, decorated with elliptical of [fluorescent lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorescent_light "Fluorescent light") and is rotated by an electric motor whilst illuminated. It is intended to represent the Buddhist quest for questions without answers, the [Kōan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dan "Kōan"). The _Koan_ was made in 1971 as part of the Peter Stuyvesant Foundation City Sculpture Project and was originally sited in Plymouth; it moved to the [Hayward Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery") in London before being purchased by Warwick in 1972.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Lijn-50)

The _Koan_ was temporarily relocated to the university's Gibbet Hill campus during refurbishments to the Warwick Arts Centre; it was returned upon completion of the project.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-52) According to student newspaper _[The Boar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boar\_(newspaper) "The Boar (newspaper)")_, the white Koan has played a role in many of campus' myths and legends – it was allegedly the nose-cap of the [Blue-Streak Missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Streak_(missile) "Blue Streak (missile)"), a supposed quick escape route for senior staff, and even a signalling device for aliens in outer space.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-theboar.org-53) The _Koan_ even garnered its own cartoon strip in the 1990s, with thirty-two episodes created by Steve Shipway.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-54) The Koan Worshipping Society, led by the Koanists, believe the _Koan_ is “the earth-bound manifestation of the immortal Koan, the creator of the universe”.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-theboar.org-53)

#### Sports facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sports facilities")]

In April 2019, the university opened a new £49 million Sports and Wellness Hub, on the main campus,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:3-56) featuring two sports halls with arena style balcony, the largest gym in the Higher education sector, a 12-lane 25 metre pool with movable floor, climbing and bouldering walls, squash courts, studio spaces and a café.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-58) The previous main sports centre was closed on 7 April 2019.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:3-56)

Elsewhere on campus is another sports hall, a £2.5 million 4-court indoor tennis centre with floodlit outdoor courts, a 400 m athletics track, multi-purpose outdoor surfaces, and over 60 acres (20 ha) of outdoor playing fields, including a football pitch and cricket grounds. Warwick was an official training venue for the [London 2012 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_2012_Olympics "London 2012 Olympics"). During the Games, some football matches were played at the nearby [Ricoh Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricoh_Arena "Ricoh Arena"), home at the time to [Coventry City Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_F.C. "Coventry City F.C."), and Warwick provided training and residential facilities for the Olympic teams.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-59)

#### Esports facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Esports facilities")]

In September 2021, Warwick opened its esports centre in the new Junction building on central campus, marking it as the first esports facility opened in a [Russell Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group") university and also the first university esports facility to be opened in the UK that is not tied to a degree.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-62) The centre is equipped with 24 PCs,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-64) and is designed to be easily configurable and moveable to facilitate the hosting of larger scale events.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-65) The centre is open to all of the public, not just students of the university, and this is all only part of "Phase 1" of a larger push from the university to invest in esports.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-66) The centre is sponsored by Uninn and Coventry City Football Club, partnered with Sky Blues in the Community, Women in Games and Special Effect and has its tech supplied by Chillblast and HyperX.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-67)

### Recent developments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Recent developments")]

In November 2005, Warwick outlined proposals for how it would like to develop its campus over the next fifteen years.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-69) The proposals built upon recent construction activity including a new [Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") and [Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics") Building, new [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science") Building, new [Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_School "Business School") buildings, a Digital Laboratory, new Residences and an expanded [Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports "Sports") Centre. The proposals envisage a shift in the "centre of gravity" of the campus away from the Students' Union towards University House and a proposed "Academic Square".

Developed projects included an inter-disciplinary biosciences research facility; a £25 million upgrade to [Warwick Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Business_School "Warwick Business School"); and the [National Automotive Innovation Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Automotive_Innovation_Campus "National Automotive Innovation Campus") (NAIC), a new £150 million venture funded by [Jaguar Land Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_Land_Rover "Jaguar Land Rover") and the UK government. The NAIC's purpose was to research and develop novel technologies to reduce dependency on fossil fuels and to reduce CO 2 emissions. The new 30,000 sq ft (2,800 m 2) campus for postgraduates was opened in early-2020. The campus has been dubbed a "brain trust" and is intended to pioneer the green and high-tech sports and luxury cars of tomorrow, doubling the size of Jaguar's research team.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-70)

In 2017, the university announced its intention to see an exponential growth of its main campus in order to remain "world-class" and cope with the growing number of applications it receives each year, especially from non-UK students.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-auto-71) This growth included a new £33 million Faculty of Arts, a £55 million new sports centre which was finished in April 2019, a new £54.3 million Interdisciplinary Biomedical Research Building (IBRB), a new type of student accommodation called "Cryfield Village", the expansion of [Warwick Manufacturing Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Manufacturing_Group "Warwick Manufacturing Group") (WMG), a redevelopment for the Art centre and a new Library.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-warwick.ac.uk-72) For this occasion, [Vice-Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-Chancellor "Vice-Chancellor") of Warwick University [Stuart Croft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Croft_(political_scientist) "Stuart Croft (political scientist)") declared: "New buildings are and will continue to be a part of our everyday existence. We need to open one new academic building a year from now until at least 2023. In order to do this and to keep Warwick as one of the world’s leading universities, we need to do this together, involving the whole community."[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-warwick.ac.uk-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-auto-71)

Warwick is governed by two formal bodies: the Council and the Senate. In addition to these, a steering committee provide strategic leadership in between meetings of the formal bodies. Faculties are overseen by faculty boards which report to the Senate.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-74) The principal officers of the university have responsibility for day-to-day operations of the university. These include the registrar, the University secretary, the group finance director, the director of commercial, the chief information and transformation officer, and the chief communications officer.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-75) The latter two roles were created after it emerged that the current registrar, Rachel Sandby-Thomas, had failed in her duty as the then data protection officer to notify staff, students, and partners of a series of significant breaches.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-76)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Finances")]

In the financial year ending 31 July 2024, the University of Warwick had a total income of £850.5 million (2022/23 – £828.2 million) and total expenditure of £559.6 million (2022/23 – £722.1 million).[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-annacc24-78) Key sources of income included £459.6 million from tuition fees and education contracts (2022/23 – £453.8 million), £74.1 million from funding body grants (2022/23 – £74.4 million), £146.5 million from research grants and contracts (2022/23 – £144.1 million), £24 million from investment income (2022/23 – £14.5 million) and £4.5 million from donations and endowments (2022/23 – £3.9 million).[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-annacc24-78)

At year end, Warwick had endowments of £7.3 million (2023 – £6.7 million) and total net assets of £733.3 million (2023 – £444.7 million).[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-annacc24-78)

### Coat of arms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Coat of arms")]

Warwick's [coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms") depicts atoms of two [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope") of [lithium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium "Lithium"), a [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") helix to represent science and also the _Bear and Ragged Staff_, historically associated with [Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwickshire "Warwickshire") and previously the [Earls of Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Warwick "Earls of Warwick") as well as the Elephant and Castle of [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry"). The Bear is not chained in the current depiction of the university's coat of arms, although it had been in its original grant of [Letters Patent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_Patent "Letters Patent") by the [College of Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arms "College of Arms").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-80)

## Academic profile

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Academic profile")]

In 2024/25, Warwick's student body consisted of 27,880 students, composed of 19,475 undergraduates and 8,405 postgraduate students.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-HESA_citation-3) About 43% of the student body comes from outside the UK and over 120 countries are represented on the campus.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Univ_Profile_People-81) The university has twenty-nine academic departments and over forty research centres and institutes, in three faculties: [Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts"), Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics ([STEM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STEM "STEM")), and Social Sciences. There were 2,492 academic and research staff in October 2018.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Univ_Profile_People-81)

Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Education "Department for Education"), with the average undergraduate entrant to the university in recent years amassing between 153–157 [UCAS Tariff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff") points in their top three pre-university qualifications – the equivalent of A*AA to A*A*A at [A-Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level_(United_Kingdom) "A-level (United Kingdom)").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Mean_Tariff-105) Based on 2022/23 [HESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Statistics_Agency "Higher Education Statistics Agency") entry standards data published in domestic league tables, which include a broad range of qualifications beyond the top three exam grades, the average student at the University of Warwick achieved 168 points – the 18th highest in the country.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-CUG_Entry-103) The university gave offers of admission to 62% of its undergraduate applicants in 2022, the 34th lowest offer rate across the country.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-112) For 2017 entry, the university was one of only a few mainstream universities (along with [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), [Imperial College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College_London "Imperial College London"), [LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"), [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), [St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews"), and [UCL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London")) to have no courses available in [Clearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS#Confirmation_and_clearing "UCAS").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-113)

22% of Warwick's undergraduates are [privately educated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_school_(United_Kingdom) "Independent school (United Kingdom)"), the fifteenth highest proportion amongst mainstream British universities.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-114) In the 2016–17 academic year, the university had a domicile breakdown of 66:9:25 of UK:EU:non-EU students respectively with a female to male ratio of 50:50.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-115)

### Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Library")]

The main university library is located in the middle of the main campus. It houses approximately 1,265,000 books[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-116) and over 13 kilometres of archives and manuscripts. The main library houses services to support Research and Teaching practice and collaboration between departments. The [Wolfson Research Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfson_Research_Exchange "Wolfson Research Exchange") opened in October 2008 and provides collaboration spaces, seminar rooms, conference facilities and study areas for Postgraduate Research students. The Teaching Grid, which opened in 2008, is a flexible space which allows teaching staff to try out new technologies and techniques. Adjacent to the main library building is the [Modern Records Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Records_Centre "Modern Records Centre"), a sizeable archive collection, including the UK's largest industrial relations collection.

### CCRU

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: CCRU")]

Main article: [Cybernetic Culture Research Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybernetic_Culture_Research_Unit "Cybernetic Culture Research Unit")

The Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (**CCRU**, sometimes typeset **Ccru**) was an experimental [cultural theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_theorist "Cultural theorist") collective formed in late 1995 at [Warwick University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_University "Warwick University"), England[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-117) which gradually separated from academia until it dissolved in the early 2000s. It garnered reputation for its idiosyncratic and surreal "theory-fiction" which incorporated [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy"), [cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk "Cyberpunk"), and [occultism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occultism "Occultism"), and its work has since had an online [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") related to the rise in popularity of [accelerationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerationism "Accelerationism").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:0-99)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-beckett-118)

The CCRU are strongly associated with former leading members [Sadie Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadie_Plant "Sadie Plant"), [Mark Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Fisher "Mark Fisher") and [Nick Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Land "Nick Land").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-119)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-120) Established at the University of Warwick philosophy department, the group listed their interests as "cinema, complexity, currencies, dance music, e-cash, encryption, feminism, fiction, images, inorganic life, jungle, markets, matrices, microbiotics, multimedia, networks, numbers, perception, replication, sex, simulation, sound, telecommunications, textiles, texts, trade, video, virtuality, war". [Iain Hamilton Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Hamilton_Grant "Iain Hamilton Grant") notes _[Neuromancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer "Neuromancer")_ as particularly influential to the group's formation.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-beckett-118) In addition to drawing inspiration from [Gilles Deleuze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Deleuze "Gilles Deleuze") and [Félix Guattari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Guattari "Félix Guattari")'s _[Anti-Oedipus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Oedipus "Anti-Oedipus")_ and _[A Thousand Plateaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Thousand\_Plateaus "A Thousand Plateaus")_, to which references can be found in the CCRU's writings, the collective drew inspiration from writers including [H. P. Lovecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._P._Lovecraft "H. P. Lovecraft"), [William Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gibson "William Gibson"), [J. G. Ballard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._G._Ballard "J. G. Ballard"), [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche "Friedrich Nietzsche"), [Octavia Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octavia_E._Butler "Octavia E. Butler"), [William S. Burroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Burroughs "William S. Burroughs"), [Carl Jung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Jung "Carl Jung").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-mit-121) Fisher described the CCRU's work as "a kind of exuberant anti-politics, a 'technihilo' celebration of the irrelevance of human agency, partly inspired by the pro-markets, anti-capitalism line developed by [Manuel DeLanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_DeLanda "Manuel DeLanda") out of [Braudel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braudel "Braudel"), and from the section of _Anti-Oedipus_ that talks about marketization as the 'revolutionary path.'"[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:0-99) Their later work drew upon [occultism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occultism "Occultism"), [esotericism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_esotericism "Western esotericism"), [numerology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerology "Numerology"), and the work of Lovecraft and [Aleister Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleister_Crowley "Aleister Crowley").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-beckett-118)

Roc Jiménez de Cisneros considers the CCRU's work to be influential on the development of [speculative realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speculative_realism "Speculative realism"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-122) while Fisher considered speculative realism to be returning to the CCRU's areas of interest in 2010.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-:0-99) In 2017, the CCRU was labeled by _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ as influential in computer science, philosophy, occultism, and cyberpunk, and credited with the creation of accelerationism.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-123)

## Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Research")]

In 2013, Warwick had a total research income of £90.1 million, of which £33.9 million was from Research Councils; £25.9 million was from central government, local authorities and public corporations; £12.7 million was from the European Union; £7.9 million was from UK industry and commerce; £5.2 million was from UK charitable bodies; £4.0 million was from overseas sources; and £0.5 million was from other sources.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-annacc-1) In the 2014 UK [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework") (REF), Warwick was again ranked 7th overall amongst multi-faculty institutions and was the top-ranked university in the Midlands.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-RAE_2008-124) 87% of the university's academic staff were rated as being in "world-leading" or "internationally excellent" departments with top research ratings of 4* or 3*.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-RAE_2008-124)

Warwick is particularly strong in the areas of decision sciences research including [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics"), [finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finance "Finance"), [management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management "Management"), [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") and [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics"). For instance, researchers of Warwick Business School have won the highest prize of the prestigious European Case Clearing House.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-125) Warwick has also established a number of stand-alone units to manage and extract commercial value from its research activities. The four most prominent examples of these units are [University of Warwick Science Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick_Science_Park "University of Warwick Science Park"); [Warwick HRI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_HRI "Warwick HRI"); Warwick Ventures; and [WMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMG_(formerly_Warwick_Manufacturing_Group) "WMG (formerly Warwick Manufacturing Group)").

### Commercial focus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Commercial focus")]

Warwick's administration has received criticism for being too aligned with business interests, at the expense of the rights and interests of students and staff. The most famous proponent of this critique was the noted historian [E. P. Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._P._Thompson "E. P. Thompson"), who edited and wrote much of _Warwick University Ltd_ in 1971.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-126) The book focuses on the debate over proposals for a social building, the brief student occupation of the Registry in 1967, and the files on surveillance of student and staff that this discovered and published.

Nevertheless, with the appointment of [Sir Nicholas Scheele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Scheele "Nick Scheele") as Chancellor in 2002, the university signalled that it intended to continue and expand its commercial activities. In an interview for the BBC, Scheele said: "I think in the future, education and industry need to become even more closely linked than they have been historically. As government funding changes, the replacement could well come through private funding from companies, individuals and grant-giving agencies."[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-127)

## Student life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Student life")]

The university has a campus cat named Rolf.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-Campus_Cat-128)

### Students' Union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Students' Union")]

Main article: [University of Warwick Students' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick_Students'_Union "University of Warwick Students' Union")

The University of Warwick Students' Union is one of the largest [students' unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Students'_union "Students' union") in the UK, with over 260 societies and 67 sports clubs including basketball, [rowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick_Boat_Club "University of Warwick Boat Club") and ice hockey. The Union has an annual turnover of approximately £6 million, the profit from which is used to provide services to students and to employ its staff and [sabbatical officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbatical_officer "Sabbatical officer"). The Union is divided into two buildings—SUHQ and The Union Building. The Union Building contains a three-room club venue known as "The Copper Rooms"; CAMRA-accredited "The Dirty Duck" pub; a popular bar called "The Terrace Bar"; Curiositea, a tea shop known for its hot chocolates, cakes and vintage atmosphere; The Graduate, a postgraduate social and study space;[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-129) and The Food Station, formerly called The Bread Oven.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-130)

Student media at Warwick includes:

### _University Challenge_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: University Challenge")]

The university won BBC television's _[University Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University\_Challenge "University Challenge")_ competition in 2021.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-132) This was their second win – their first was in 2007, beating the title-holders [University of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester "University of Manchester") in the final.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-133)

### Esports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Esports")]

The University of Warwick are the seven-time UK Esports "University of the Year", having won the title every year since its inception.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-134) In August 2022, Warwick became the first UK university to receive a finalist nomination for the Esports Awards, for Esports Collegiate Program of the Year, with Head of Esports Jack Fenton also becoming the first UK nominee for Collegiate Ambassador of the Year.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-135) Warwick fields numerous esports teams each year through its student-run esports society, Warwick Esports, who compete out of the Esports Centre.

### Student housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Student housing")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Sherbourne%2C_University_of_Warwick.jpg/250px-Sherbourne%2C_University_of_Warwick.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sherbourne,_University_of_Warwick.jpg)

One of the Sherbourne residences

The Warwick campus currently has around 6,300 student bedrooms across a range of undergraduate and postgraduate residences. All of the residences are self-catered, and each has residential tutors and a warden.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-136) Warwick guarantees accommodation for all first-year undergraduate students, regardless of their present address. Many of the university's postgraduate population are also catered for, with some specific residences available for postgraduate living. Each residence accommodates a mixture of students both with home and international status, male and female, and, sometimes, undergraduate and postgraduate.

In their second and third years, many students live in one of the surrounding towns: either Coventry, Canley, Kenilworth or Royal Leamington Spa, where they can live in student accommodation or independently owned residences. Since 2011, Warwick has constructed two new halls of residences for the students. Bluebell, opened in 2011, offers accommodation in flats of eight people, with a total of 505 single rooms for first-year undergraduates. The Sherbourne residences was opened in 2012, which similarly provides 527 ensuite rooms to first-years,[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-137) and was extended with a further 267 rooms in 2017.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-138) A further 700 new rooms were built in the Cryfield Village, namely Cryfield ‘Townhouse’ and ‘Standard’ residences.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-139)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-140)

### Political incidents

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Warwick&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Political incidents")]

In June 2014, the university announced [Alex Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Davies_(extremist) "Alex Davies (extremist)"), a member of the proscribed terrorist organisation [National Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Action_(UK) "National Action (UK)"), voluntarily withdrew from his course.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-141) In early 2018, it was reported that a group of male students had constituted a group chat in which many references to rape, occasionally targeted at particular other students, and other sexual offences were made, in such a way which left significant cause for concern.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-142) As a result of this and other incidents, students staged a [sit-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sit-in "Sit-in") in 2021 in the central plaza of the university.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-143) In January 2020, the university was criticised for choosing not to adopt the [IHRA definition of antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Definition_of_Antisemitism "Working Definition of Antisemitism"). This decision was later reversed in October following intervention by Education Secretary [Gavin Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Williamson "Gavin Williamson").[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick#cite_note-144)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[Universities in Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_in_Bangladesh "Universities in Bangladesh") are mainly categorized into four differential types: [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university") (government owned and subsidized), [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university") (private sector owned universities), [international](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_university "International university") (operated and funded by [international organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization") such as the [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation")), and the latest Cross Border Higher Education (CBHE) which are either study centres or branch campuses managed by of top universities in the world. Bangladeshi universities are affiliated with the [University Grants Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Grants_Commission_of_Bangladesh "University Grants Commission of Bangladesh"), a commission created according to the Presidential Order (P.O. No 10 of 1973) of the government of the [People's Republic of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-1)

Most universities focus on [general studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_studies "General studies"), mixing together such areas of study as [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_studies "Business studies"), [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_education "Engineering education") and [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_education "Technology education"). Twenty-two universities have specialized curricula. Two of these are focused on [Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_studies "Islamic studies"), four on [health science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_science "Health science"), six on [agricultural science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_science "Agricultural science"), six on engineering, one on [textile engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_engineering "Textile engineering"), one on [Veterinary medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_medicine "Veterinary medicine"), one on [Aeronautical science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_science "Aeronautical science"), one on [ocean science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_science "Ocean science") and one on [women's studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_studies "Women's studies").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-2)

## Public universities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Public universities")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg/250px-BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg)

Locations of Public Universities in Bangladesh

Bangladesh has 60[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-3) public universities to the bulk of higher studies students. These universities are funded by the government while managed as self-governed organizations.

[Dhaka Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_Division "Dhaka Division") is home to 21 public universities, among which 11 are in [Dhaka City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka"). There are nine public universities in [Chittagong Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division"), the [Khulna Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khulna_Division "Khulna Division") has seven, [Rajshahi Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajshahi_Division "Rajshahi Division") has six, each of [Mymensingh Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mymensingh_Division "Mymensingh Division"), [Rangpur Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangpur_Division "Rangpur Division") and [Sylhet Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet_Division "Sylhet Division") has four. And [Barisal Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barisal_Division "Barisal Division") has three. As of 2022 the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh has introduced the cluster system for students enrollment. According to this system all [public universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_universities "Public universities") in Bangladesh should be sorted in five clusters i.e. one for agricultural universities; one for science and technology universities, one for engineering universities, one for [medical universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_universities "Medical universities") and the last one for general studies universities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-6)

## International universities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: International universities")]

There are only three international universities in Bangladesh according to UGC. They are neither managed nor funded by the government, like public universities, nor established under the Private University Act and managed by a private governing body, like private universities. International Culture University, established by civil society organization and branded by United Nations Academic Impact (UNAI)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-154) and United Nations Global Compact (UNGC),[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-155) is an internationally accredited-affiliated and an active partner of different international organizations working for internationalization of education and international quality. Islamic University of Technology was established by the [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation") and is located in [Gazipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazipur,_Dhaka_Division "Gazipur, Dhaka Division"), another is located in [Chittagong Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division") and funded by the Asian University for Women Support Foundation (AUWSF), a United States–based non-profit corporation.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-156) later one is South Asian University.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-157)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[Universities in Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_in_Bangladesh "Universities in Bangladesh") are mainly categorized into four differential types: [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university") (government owned and subsidized), [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university") (private sector owned universities), [international](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_university "International university") (operated and funded by [international organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization") such as the [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation")), and the latest Cross Border Higher Education (CBHE) which are either study centres or branch campuses managed by of top universities in the world. Bangladeshi universities are affiliated with the [University Grants Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Grants_Commission_of_Bangladesh "University Grants Commission of Bangladesh"), a commission created according to the Presidential Order (P.O. No 10 of 1973) of the government of the [People's Republic of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-1)

Most universities focus on [general studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_studies "General studies"), mixing together such areas of study as [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_studies "Business studies"), [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_education "Engineering education") and [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_education "Technology education"). Twenty-two universities have specialized curricula. Two of these are focused on [Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_studies "Islamic studies"), four on [health science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_science "Health science"), six on [agricultural science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_science "Agricultural science"), six on engineering, one on [textile engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_engineering "Textile engineering"), one on [Veterinary medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_medicine "Veterinary medicine"), one on [Aeronautical science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_science "Aeronautical science"), one on [ocean science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_science "Ocean science") and one on [women's studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_studies "Women's studies").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-2)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg/250px-BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BangaldeshPublicUniversitiesLocation.jpg)

Locations of Public Universities in Bangladesh

Bangladesh has 60[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-3) public universities to the bulk of higher studies students. These universities are funded by the government while managed as self-governed organizations.

[Dhaka Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_Division "Dhaka Division") is home to 21 public universities, among which 11 are in [Dhaka City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka"). There are nine public universities in [Chittagong Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division"), the [Khulna Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khulna_Division "Khulna Division") has seven, [Rajshahi Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajshahi_Division "Rajshahi Division") has six, each of [Mymensingh Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mymensingh_Division "Mymensingh Division"), [Rangpur Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangpur_Division "Rangpur Division") and [Sylhet Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet_Division "Sylhet Division") has four. And [Barisal Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barisal_Division "Barisal Division") has three. As of 2022 the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh has introduced the cluster system for students enrollment. According to this system all [public universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_universities "Public universities") in Bangladesh should be sorted in five clusters i.e. one for agricultural universities; one for science and technology universities, one for engineering universities, one for [medical universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_universities "Medical universities") and the last one for general studies universities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-6)

## International universities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: International universities")]

There are only three international universities in Bangladesh according to UGC. They are neither managed nor funded by the government, like public universities, nor established under the Private University Act and managed by a private governing body, like private universities. International Culture University, established by civil society organization and branded by United Nations Academic Impact (UNAI)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-154) and United Nations Global Compact (UNGC),[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-155) is an internationally accredited-affiliated and an active partner of different international organizations working for internationalization of education and international quality. Islamic University of Technology was established by the [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation") and is located in [Gazipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazipur,_Dhaka_Division "Gazipur, Dhaka Division"), another is located in [Chittagong Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division") and funded by the Asian University for Women Support Foundation (AUWSF), a United States–based non-profit corporation.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-156) later one is South Asian University.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-157)

The **Eastern University** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): [ইস্টার্ন ইউনিভার্সিটি](https://bn.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E0%A6%87%E0%A6%B8%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%9F%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%B0%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%A8%20%E0%A6%87%E0%A6%89%E0%A6%A8%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%AD%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%B0%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%B8%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%9F%E0%A6%BF "bn:ইস্টার্ন ইউনিভার্সিটি")) is a private university located in Ashulia, [Savar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savar "Savar"), Dhaka, Bangladesh. The Eastern University was established in 2003 under the Private University Act 1992, and later on approved under Private University Act of 2010. The university was set up by Eastern University Foundation.

The university campus is located on Road 6, Block B, Ashulia Model Town, Savar, Dhaka-1345. The university campus covers about 8 acres of land.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Schools and Departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Schools and Departments")]

The university has five Schools: School of Arts, School of Business, School of Engineering, School of Law an School of Life Science]. The School of Arts has one departments – the Department of English. The School of Business has four major areas, namely, Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Management, and Human Resource. The School of Business at Eastern University has come up with the BBA Program in Islamic Finance, Banking and Insurance. A few social science courses are also offered by the School. The School of Engineering has three departments, namely the Department of Computer Science & Information Technology, the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering and the Civil Engineering. The School of Law has an undergraduate and postgraduate program. The School of Science - The Department of Pharmacy. Approval of the Department of Textile Engineering is under consideration by UGC.

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

Eastern University follows the North American model of the curriculum in the fields of Business Administration, Computer Science and Electrical and Electronics Engineering, the UK model in Law and English. The academic program is pursued through a curriculum that includes splitting up of an academic year into two semesters: the Spring and the Summer.

### Session

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Session")]

The academic session of EU is a three-semester cycle: Spring, Summer and Fall.

### Faculty members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Faculty members")]

The university has 231 full-time and part-time faculty members out of which 47 are Ph.D. including a visiting professor from the United States.

## Research and publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Research and publications")]

The university has a research center known as the [Centre for Research and Development](https://www.easternuni.edu.bd/centre-for-research-and-development). In addition to facilitating research studies and consultancy projects, it organizes research, seminars and training on research methodology. The university publishes a biannual refereed journal - _The Eastern University Journal_.
