The **Eastern University** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): [ইস্টার্ন ইউনিভার্সিটি](https://bn.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E0%A6%87%E0%A6%B8%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%9F%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%B0%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%A8%20%E0%A6%87%E0%A6%89%E0%A6%A8%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%AD%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%B0%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%B8%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%9F%E0%A6%BF "bn:ইস্টার্ন ইউনিভার্সিটি")) is a private university located in Ashulia, [Savar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savar "Savar"), Dhaka, Bangladesh. The Eastern University was established in 2003 under the Private University Act 1992, and later on approved under Private University Act of 2010. The university was set up by Eastern University Foundation.

## Schools and Departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Schools and Departments")]

The university has five Schools: School of Arts, School of Business, School of Engineering, School of Law an School of Life Science]. The School of Arts has one departments – the Department of English. The School of Business has four major areas, namely, Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Management, and Human Resource. The School of Business at Eastern University has come up with the BBA Program in Islamic Finance, Banking and Insurance. A few social science courses are also offered by the School. The School of Engineering has three departments, namely the Department of Computer Science & Information Technology, the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering and the Civil Engineering. The School of Law has an undergraduate and postgraduate program. The School of Science - The Department of Pharmacy. Approval of the Department of Textile Engineering is under consideration by UGC.

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

Eastern University follows the North American model of the curriculum in the fields of Business Administration, Computer Science and Electrical and Electronics Engineering, the UK model in Law and English. The academic program is pursued through a curriculum that includes splitting up of an academic year into two semesters: the Spring and the Summer.

### Session

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Session")]

The academic session of EU is a three-semester cycle: Spring, Summer and Fall.

### Faculty members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Faculty members")]

The university has 231 full-time and part-time faculty members out of which 47 are Ph.D. including a visiting professor from the United States.

## Research and publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eastern_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Research and publications")]

The university has a research center known as the [Centre for Research and Development](https://www.easternuni.edu.bd/centre-for-research-and-development). In addition to facilitating research studies and consultancy projects, it organizes research, seminars and training on research methodology. The university publishes a biannual refereed journal - _The Eastern University Journal_.

## History and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and administration")]

Southeast University (SEU) was established in June 2002 as a private university under the Private University Act 1992. The [President of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bangladesh "President of Bangladesh") is the chancellor. The university is run by a number of statutory bodies as required under the provisions of the Private University Act, 1992.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-7)

## Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Library")]

Southeast University is linked with journal publishers through an international organisation named INASP/PERii. [Bangladesh Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Academy_of_Sciences "Bangladesh Academy of Sciences") (BAS) is acting as the coordinating body. This facility is IP based and work only within SEU campus. The SEU library offers regular services such as circulation, reference, counseling, indexing, bibliographical documentation, back up services, retrospective searches etc.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-12)

Southeast University has a library equipped with books on the academic programs offered as well as on research and extracurricular activities. The total collection of books and journals at is about 15000. The space area of the library is 6,500 square feet (600 m 2). It is a central library of the university rendering services to the students and faculty.

## Terms and grading

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Terms and grading")]

Southeast University is modeled on the North American _Open Credit_ system. It maintains tri-semester (term) year with the exception of the Department of Pharmacy which maintains a bi-semester year. Southeast University semester timeline is as follow:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-13)

*   Spring: January - April (starting on the second Sunday of January)
*   Summer: May - August (starting on the second Sunday of May)
*   Fall: September - December (starting on the second Sunday of September)

Letter grades indicating the quality of course work completed are interpreted as follows:[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-Grading_Scheme-14)

| Class Intervals of Scores | Letter Grade | Grade Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80 – 100 | A+ | 4.00 |
| 75 - 79 | A | 3.75 |
| 70 – 74 | A- | 3.50 |
| 65 – 69 | B+ | 3.25 |
| 60 – 64 | B | 3.00 |
| 55 - 59 | B- | 2.75 |
| 50 – 54 | C+ | 2.50 |
| 45 – 49 | C | 2.25 |
| 40 – 44 | D | 2.00 |
| Less than 40 | F | 0.00 |

Traditional class equivalent as per MOE, GOB, notification dated 02.06.2009: GPA 3.00-4.00= 1st class GPA 2.25-2.99= 2nd class GPA 1.65-2.24= 3rd class

## Scholarships opportunities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Scholarships opportunities")]

SEU offers partial to full tuition fee waiver based on outstanding [HSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Secondary_School_Certificate "Higher Secondary School Certificate") or [A-Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level "A-level") result. But the result based waiver is not applicable in case of break of study. Also each semester the top ranked students from every department based on semester GPA gets partial financial assistance. Limited need based financial assistance program is available for students with more than 3.00 semester GPA. Children of Freedom Fighters are eligible for full tuition waiver & it remains valid in the subsequent semesters if the semester result is within the requirement.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-15)

**Southeast University** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): সাউথইস্ট বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়) is a private university in [Tejgaon Industrial Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tejgaon_Industrial_Area_Thana "Tejgaon Industrial Area Thana"), [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"). The university was established in 2002.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-3) SEU ranked 10th among Top Private universities in Dhaka Tribune's Private University Ranking 2019.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-4)

## History and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and administration")]

Southeast University (SEU) was established in June 2002 as a private university under the Private University Act 1992. The [President of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bangladesh "President of Bangladesh") is the chancellor. The university is run by a number of statutory bodies as required under the provisions of the Private University Act, 1992.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-7)

## Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Library")]

Southeast University is linked with journal publishers through an international organisation named INASP/PERii. [Bangladesh Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Academy_of_Sciences "Bangladesh Academy of Sciences") (BAS) is acting as the coordinating body. This facility is IP based and work only within SEU campus. The SEU library offers regular services such as circulation, reference, counseling, indexing, bibliographical documentation, back up services, retrospective searches etc.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-12)

Southeast University has a library equipped with books on the academic programs offered as well as on research and extracurricular activities. The total collection of books and journals at is about 15000. The space area of the library is 6,500 square feet (600 m 2). It is a central library of the university rendering services to the students and faculty.

## Terms and grading

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Terms and grading")]

Southeast University is modeled on the North American _Open Credit_ system. It maintains tri-semester (term) year with the exception of the Department of Pharmacy which maintains a bi-semester year. Southeast University semester timeline is as follow:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-13)

*   Spring: January - April (starting on the second Sunday of January)
*   Summer: May - August (starting on the second Sunday of May)
*   Fall: September - December (starting on the second Sunday of September)

Letter grades indicating the quality of course work completed are interpreted as follows:[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-Grading_Scheme-14)

| Class Intervals of Scores | Letter Grade | Grade Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80 – 100 | A+ | 4.00 |
| 75 - 79 | A | 3.75 |
| 70 – 74 | A- | 3.50 |
| 65 – 69 | B+ | 3.25 |
| 60 – 64 | B | 3.00 |
| 55 - 59 | B- | 2.75 |
| 50 – 54 | C+ | 2.50 |
| 45 – 49 | C | 2.25 |
| 40 – 44 | D | 2.00 |
| Less than 40 | F | 0.00 |

Traditional class equivalent as per MOE, GOB, notification dated 02.06.2009: GPA 3.00-4.00= 1st class GPA 2.25-2.99= 2nd class GPA 1.65-2.24= 3rd class

## Scholarships opportunities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Scholarships opportunities")]

SEU offers partial to full tuition fee waiver based on outstanding [HSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Secondary_School_Certificate "Higher Secondary School Certificate") or [A-Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level "A-level") result. But the result based waiver is not applicable in case of break of study. Also each semester the top ranked students from every department based on semester GPA gets partial financial assistance. Limited need based financial assistance program is available for students with more than 3.00 semester GPA. Children of Freedom Fighters are eligible for full tuition waiver & it remains valid in the subsequent semesters if the semester result is within the requirement.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_University_(Bangladesh)#cite_note-15)

The **University of Information Technology & Sciences** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): ইউনিভার্সিটি অব ইনফরমেশন টেকনোলজি অ্যান্ড সায়েন্সেস) commonly known as **UITS** is a private university in [Baridhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baridhara "Baridhara"), [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-history-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The UITS was founded on August 7, 2003, as a non-profit organization. Information Science and Technology Solution Ltd., a concern of [PHP Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PHP_Family "PHP Family") headed by Alhaj Sufi Mohamed Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury is the sponsor of UITS.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-history-2)

## Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Administration")]

The vice chancellor of the university is the chief executive. Each academic department has its own head. On top of the administration, there is the Board of Trustees (BoT), headed by a chairperson, which oversees policy matters. In the academic sphere, the highest authority is vested in the Academic Council represented by heads of schools and teaching departments, representatives of teachers and nominated members who are associated with education, science, culture, industries, media and scientific and cultural organizations in the country. The council is presided over by the vice chancellor. The registrar of the university acts as the secretary who is also the custodian of the university seal.

The university has shifted to a fully equipped permanent campus on November 11, 2019, situated at Nayanagar, Vatara, Dhaka. The campus started its journey right after the freshers ceremony of Autumn Semester, 2019.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-4)

## Timeline of UITS

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Timeline of UITS")]

*   On August 7, 2003, the university began with 3 schools.
*   On March 10, 2004, the Bachelor of Business Administration, the first undergraduate program of UITS, was started under Business Studies Department.
*   On August 22, 2004, the Bachelor of Arts in English and Master of Computer Applications was started under Department of English and Computer Science & Engineering.
*   On October 18, 2004, the International Master of Business Administration was started under Business Studies Department
*   On September 13, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Science in Computer Science & Engineering was started under Department of Computer Science & Engineering.
*   On October 9, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Science in Electronics & Communication Engineering and the Master of Science in Telecommunications were started under the Department of Electronics & Communication Engineering.
*   On November 20, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Laws was started under the Department of Law.
*   On March 22, 2006, the programme Master of Laws was started under the Department of Law. Master of Arts in English was started under the Department of English, and Bachelor of Science in Information Technology was started under Department of Information Technology.
*   On May 3, 2006, the programme Master of Science in Telecommunication was started under the Department of Electronic & Communication Engineering.
*   On July 27, 2008, the programme Bachelor of Laws (2 years) was started under the Department of Law.
*   On December 21, 2008, the programme Bachelor of Science in Electrical & Electronic Engineering was started under the Department of Electrical & Electronic Engineering.
*   On May 7, 2012, the programme Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering was started under the Department of Civil Engineering.
*   On October 22, 2013, the programme Bachelor of Social Sciences in Social Work and Master of Social Sciences in Social Work was started under the Department of Social Work.
*   On December 3, 2013, the programme Bachelor of Pharmacy was started under the Department of Pharmacy.
*   In October 2018 the programme Bachelor of Pharmacy was accredited by the Pharmacy Council of Bangladesh (PCB).

The **University of Information Technology & Sciences** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): ইউনিভার্সিটি অব ইনফরমেশন টেকনোলজি অ্যান্ড সায়েন্সেস) commonly known as **UITS** is a private university in [Baridhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baridhara "Baridhara"), [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-history-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The UITS was founded on August 7, 2003, as a non-profit organization. Information Science and Technology Solution Ltd., a concern of [PHP Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PHP_Family "PHP Family") headed by Alhaj Sufi Mohamed Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury is the sponsor of UITS.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences#cite_note-history-2)

## Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Administration")]

The vice chancellor of the university is the chief executive. Each academic department has its own head. On top of the administration, there is the Board of Trustees (BoT), headed by a chairperson, which oversees policy matters. In the academic sphere, the highest authority is vested in the Academic Council represented by heads of schools and teaching departments, representatives of teachers and nominated members who are associated with education, science, culture, industries, media and scientific and cultural organizations in the country. The council is presided over by the vice chancellor. The registrar of the university acts as the secretary who is also the custodian of the university seal.

## Timeline of UITS

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Information_Technology_and_Sciences&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Timeline of UITS")]

*   On August 7, 2003, the university began with 3 schools.
*   On March 10, 2004, the Bachelor of Business Administration, the first undergraduate program of UITS, was started under Business Studies Department.
*   On August 22, 2004, the Bachelor of Arts in English and Master of Computer Applications was started under Department of English and Computer Science & Engineering.
*   On October 18, 2004, the International Master of Business Administration was started under Business Studies Department
*   On September 13, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Science in Computer Science & Engineering was started under Department of Computer Science & Engineering.
*   On October 9, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Science in Electronics & Communication Engineering and the Master of Science in Telecommunications were started under the Department of Electronics & Communication Engineering.
*   On November 20, 2005, the programme Bachelor of Laws was started under the Department of Law.
*   On March 22, 2006, the programme Master of Laws was started under the Department of Law. Master of Arts in English was started under the Department of English, and Bachelor of Science in Information Technology was started under Department of Information Technology.
*   On May 3, 2006, the programme Master of Science in Telecommunication was started under the Department of Electronic & Communication Engineering.
*   On July 27, 2008, the programme Bachelor of Laws (2 years) was started under the Department of Law.
*   On December 21, 2008, the programme Bachelor of Science in Electrical & Electronic Engineering was started under the Department of Electrical & Electronic Engineering.
*   On May 7, 2012, the programme Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering was started under the Department of Civil Engineering.
*   On October 22, 2013, the programme Bachelor of Social Sciences in Social Work and Master of Social Sciences in Social Work was started under the Department of Social Work.
*   On December 3, 2013, the programme Bachelor of Pharmacy was started under the Department of Pharmacy.
*   In October 2018 the programme Bachelor of Pharmacy was accredited by the Pharmacy Council of Bangladesh (PCB).

Bangladeshi industrialist

**Sufi Mohammed Mizanur Rahman** is a distinguished Bangladeshi industrialist and social worker, renowned as the founding chairman of the [PHP Group of Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PHP_Family "PHP Family"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-1) a prominent Bangladeshi conglomerate. In recognition of his outstanding contributions to social welfare and industrial development, the government of Bangladesh conferred upon him the [Ekushey Padak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekushey_Padak "Ekushey Padak"), the nation's second-highest civilian honor, in 2020.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-2)

In May 2025, an attempted murder case was filed against Rahman over a student of Alia Madrasa getting injured in [Old Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dhaka "Old Dhaka") during protests against Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-3)

**Sufi Mohammed Mizanur Rahman** is a distinguished Bangladeshi industrialist and social worker, renowned as the founding chairman of the [PHP Group of Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PHP_Family "PHP Family"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-1) a prominent Bangladeshi conglomerate. In recognition of his outstanding contributions to social welfare and industrial development, the government of Bangladesh conferred upon him the [Ekushey Padak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekushey_Padak "Ekushey Padak"), the nation's second-highest civilian honor, in 2020.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-2)

In May 2025, an attempted murder case was filed against Rahman over a student of Alia Madrasa getting injured in [Old Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dhaka "Old Dhaka") during protests against Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi_Mohammed_Mizanur_Rahman#cite_note-3)

The **University of West London** (**UWL**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-4) in the [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") with campuses in [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford") and [Reading, Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire").

The university has roots in 1860 when the **Lady Byron School** was founded, later **Ealing College of Higher Education**. In 1992, the then-named **Polytechnic of West London** became a university as **Thames Valley University** (TVU). 18 years later, after several mergers, acquisitions and campus moves, it was renamed to its current name.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-PA-Aug2010-5)

The University of West London comprises nine schools: The Claude Littner Business School, the London Geller College of Hospitality and Tourism, the School of Computing and Engineering, the [London College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_College_of_Music "London College of Music"), the College of Nursing, Midwifery and Healthcare, the School of Law, the School of Human and Social Sciences, the School of Biomedical Sciences and the London School of Film, Media and Design.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The University of West London traces its roots back to 1860 when the [Lady Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Byron "Lady Byron") School was founded at what is now the University of West London's Ealing campus. The school later became Ealing College of Higher Education.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg/250px-University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg)

Ealing College, founded in 1860 by [Lady Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Byron "Lady Byron")

The Slough campus was founded in January 1912 as a selective secondary school on William Street. By the 1960s, it had become Slough College of Further Education. In the 1960’s the St Mary’s Road site was known as Ealing Technical College, offering CNAA degrees in law (and others). In the 1980s it became Thames Valley College of Higher Education but was closed in 2011.

In 1991, Ealing College of Higher Education, Thames Valley College of Higher Education, Queen Charlotte's College of Health Care Studies and [London College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_College_of_Music "London College of Music") were merged to become the Polytechnic of West London. Two years later, the polytechnic became a university under the [Further and Higher Education Act 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Further_and_Higher_Education_Act_1992 "Further and Higher Education Act 1992") and adopted the name Thames Valley University (TVU). In 1994, the university merged with Northwick Park School of Nursing, Riverside College of Nursing and the North West Thames Regional Authority's AIDS unit. In 1995, it merged with the Berkshire College of Nursing and Midwifery.

In 2004, the university merged with Reading College and School of Arts and Design, which had been founded in 1947 as Reading Technical College. Reading College's sites at Kings Road and Crescent Road became TVU sites.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg/250px-TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg)

Paragon Campus in [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford") (former TVU branding)

In 2009, the university decided to divest itself of its [further education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Further_education "Further education") courses, together with its Kings Road site that it had inherited from the Reading College and School of Arts and Design. In May 2009, the university announced that it would be closing its Slough campus in 2010 due to the relocation of nursing students, who make up the majority of the student body there, to Reading. Other courses would be moved to one of the university's Greater London campuses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-6) In July 2009, the university was awarded the [Queen's Anniversary Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Anniversary_Prize "Queen's Anniversary Prize") for outstanding achievement and excellence in hospitality education.

In 2010 the responsibility for further education, along with the Kings Road site, was transferred to a relaunched [Reading College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_College "Reading College"). Although some 40 miles west of London, the university retained its other sites in Reading, including the Crescent Road site that also originated with Reading College and the School of Arts and Design.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-rcarc-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-rcpb-8)

In August 2010, it was announced that the university would change its name to the University of West London, with the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council "Privy Council") subsequently granting permission for the change.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-PA-Aug2010-5) The university unveiled a new logo in April 2011. Vice-chancellor Peter John stated that the changes reflected the university's development since 1992 and a new focus on its Brentford and Ealing campuses.

In 2015, a £100 million expansion of the Ealing campus was completed. This work included new facilities such as a new library, student union and updated teaching facilities - building which was highly unpopular with many of the locals.

In 2019 the university merged with [Drama Studio London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_Studio_London "Drama Studio London") in Ealing, and in 2021 it merged with [Ruskin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruskin_College "Ruskin College"), Oxford.

## Campuses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Campuses")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg/250px-TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg)

Walpole House in [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), housing the university's administration.

There are two campus sites in western Greater London, located at St Mary's Road, Ealing and Paragon House in Brentford. There is also a third site in Reading, Berkshire, which is some 35 miles (55 km) from the Ealing sites.

In 2015, the St Mary's Road, Ealing campus underwent a £100 million transformation, with a new social area, library, student union, gym and updated facilities. In 2017, a further £1M was invested in the development of the Paragon campus in Brentford and the addition of a nursing simulation centre in the Reading campus.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Ealing campus is home to The Heathrow Archive, a collection of more than 800 artefacts that tell the story of [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport")'s history from 1946 to 2016.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2017, the University of West London launched its overseas branch campus in [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), United Arab Emirates.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Organisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organisation")]

The University of West London comprises nine schools: The Claude Littner Business School, the London Geller College of Hospitality and Tourism, the School of Computing and Engineering, the London College of Music, the College of Nursing, Midwifery and Healthcare, the School of Law, the School of Human and Social Sciences, the School of Biomedical Sciences, and the London School of Film, Media and Design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-9)

The Graduate School[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-10) (based in Ealing) coordinates and provides support to research activities[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-11) and research degree courses. The University offers traditional PhD programmes and Professional Doctorates.

The university also works with the Met Film School, a private film school that is based at [Ealing Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Studios "Ealing Studios") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-SD-12) The school, which launched in 2003, offers two and three-year bachelor's programmes as well as various master's degree programmes, which are accredited through the University of West London.

In 2020, the university was ranked 34th best university (out of 130+ institutions) in the UK by the 2021 edition of _The Times_ and _Sunday Times_ Good University Guide.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 2021, the university was ranked 34th in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ university guide[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-17) and the university was named the top modern university in London in _[The Guardian University Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian\_University\_Guide "The Guardian University Guide")_ 2022.

The university was ranked 801-1000 in the _Times Higher Education_ Impact Rankings 2024 that evaluates universities worldwide based on their contributions to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). As such, within specific Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), UWL achieved the following rankings: 101-200 for Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10), 301-400 for Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12), and 801-1000 for both Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3) and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG 17).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-18)

The university recorded the best results of any university in Greater London in the annual National Student Survey (NSS) in 2016, with students' responses showing it to be the best University in Greater London for student satisfaction.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-uwl.ac.uk-19) In the NSS 2016, there were 100 per cent overall satisfaction rates for nine courses across the University's eight schools, ranging from Midwifery to Business Studies and Music Technology to Hospitality Management. Among these 100 per cent overall satisfaction rates, the University recorded the best overall satisfaction rates in the UK for Civil Engineering and Building courses in the NSS 2016.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-uwl.ac.uk-19) In 2021, UWL was named the university of the year for student experience in _The Times_ and _Sunday Times_ Good University Guide.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-20)

### Students' Union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Students' Union")]

The University of West London Students' Union (UWLSU) is the recognised student organisation of the University of West London. UWLSU is affiliated with the [National Union of Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Union_of_Students_(United_Kingdom) "National Union of Students (United Kingdom)").

The union has the ground floor of the North Building at the St. Mary's Road campus and is home to a cafe - Coffee Union and social space - Freddie's. The Sports Centre is also located on the Park Road entrance of the St. Mary's Road campus which is open exclusively to UWL staff, students, alumni, and residents that live within the local area. The union also has a space on the second floor at the Paragon campus and a third space on the 9th floor at the Reading campus.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The union aims to bring students academic advice and advocacy support, events, ways to take up new activities, and sports, and a place to socialise. With the course representative programme run by their Student Voice team, students can apply to be a course or school representative to help advocate for academic change.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Student accommodation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Student accommodation")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg/250px-University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg)

The University of West London Campus at St Mary's Road, [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing")

Before 2006, the university operated [halls of residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halls_of_residence "Halls of residence") only at the Reading campus, although several private houses in the Ealing area were rented by the university and allocated to students studying there. In September 2006 the university began to offer halls of residence accommodation to students from the Ealing and Slough campuses at a student and keyworker accommodation site named Paragon. The site won the 'Major Housing Project of the Year' category at the 2007 Building Awards, and is in [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford"), approximately two miles away from the Ealing campus.

Paragon is home to the tallest building to be completed using [modern methods of construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_methods_of_construction "Modern methods of construction") (MMC) in the UK, which serves as a 130,000 sq ft (12,000 m 2) academic facility for the university's human sciences facility. The student accommodation at Paragon had been criticised by its residents for being too expensive, costing the highest of all Greater London universities' halls of residence along with [SOAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAS "SOAS") in the 2007–2008 year. TVU defended the costs, asserting that the halls are of an especially high standard.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-22)

In 2020, [Notting Hill Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Genesis "Notting Hill Genesis"), the company that owned the Paragon student lets site, controversially closed the entire student halls of residence[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-23) due to fire safety concerns, asking students to immediately evacuate. Students were moved to temporary housing in nearby Wembley whilst the university found suitable housing. Accommodation for students at UWL now varies from shared housing to student lets in Ealing, Acton and the surrounding area.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-24)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In the mid-1990s, its high-profile vice-chancellor, [Mike Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Fitzgerald_(academic) "Mike Fitzgerald (academic)"), ushered through a networked "New Learning Environment" for undergraduate students, involving a shift to online delivery and assessment. The NLE was discontinued in this form, and Fitzgerald resigned in 1998 following a negative [Quality Assurance Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_Assurance_Agency "Quality Assurance Agency") report stating there were "significant management failures" in the delivery of this model.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-25) The University suffered severe financial shortfalls in the years that followed.

The **University of West London** (**UWL**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-4) in the [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") with campuses in [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford") and [Reading, Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire").

The university has roots in 1860 when the **Lady Byron School** was founded, later **Ealing College of Higher Education**. In 1992, the then-named **Polytechnic of West London** became a university as **Thames Valley University** (TVU). 18 years later, after several mergers, acquisitions and campus moves, it was renamed to its current name.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-PA-Aug2010-5)

The University of West London comprises nine schools: The Claude Littner Business School, the London Geller College of Hospitality and Tourism, the School of Computing and Engineering, the [London College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_College_of_Music "London College of Music"), the College of Nursing, Midwifery and Healthcare, the School of Law, the School of Human and Social Sciences, the School of Biomedical Sciences and the London School of Film, Media and Design.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The University of West London traces its roots back to 1860 when the [Lady Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Byron "Lady Byron") School was founded at what is now the University of West London's Ealing campus. The school later became Ealing College of Higher Education.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg/250px-University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_West_London_Ealing_College.jpg)

Ealing College, founded in 1860 by [Lady Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Byron "Lady Byron")

The Slough campus was founded in January 1912 as a selective secondary school on William Street. By the 1960s, it had become Slough College of Further Education. In the 1960’s the St Mary’s Road site was known as Ealing Technical College, offering CNAA degrees in law (and others). In the 1980s it became Thames Valley College of Higher Education but was closed in 2011.

In 1991, Ealing College of Higher Education, Thames Valley College of Higher Education, Queen Charlotte's College of Health Care Studies and [London College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_College_of_Music "London College of Music") were merged to become the Polytechnic of West London. Two years later, the polytechnic became a university under the [Further and Higher Education Act 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Further_and_Higher_Education_Act_1992 "Further and Higher Education Act 1992") and adopted the name Thames Valley University (TVU). In 1994, the university merged with Northwick Park School of Nursing, Riverside College of Nursing and the North West Thames Regional Authority's AIDS unit. In 1995, it merged with the Berkshire College of Nursing and Midwifery.

In 2004, the university merged with Reading College and School of Arts and Design, which had been founded in 1947 as Reading Technical College. Reading College's sites at Kings Road and Crescent Road became TVU sites.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg/250px-TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TVU_Paragon_Campus_Brentford.jpg)

Paragon Campus in [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford") (former TVU branding)

In 2009, the university decided to divest itself of its [further education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Further_education "Further education") courses, together with its Kings Road site that it had inherited from the Reading College and School of Arts and Design. In May 2009, the university announced that it would be closing its Slough campus in 2010 due to the relocation of nursing students, who make up the majority of the student body there, to Reading. Other courses would be moved to one of the university's Greater London campuses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-6) In July 2009, the university was awarded the [Queen's Anniversary Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Anniversary_Prize "Queen's Anniversary Prize") for outstanding achievement and excellence in hospitality education.

In 2010 the responsibility for further education, along with the Kings Road site, was transferred to a relaunched [Reading College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_College "Reading College"). Although some 40 miles west of London, the university retained its other sites in Reading, including the Crescent Road site that also originated with Reading College and the School of Arts and Design.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-rcarc-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-rcpb-8)

In August 2010, it was announced that the university would change its name to the University of West London, with the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council "Privy Council") subsequently granting permission for the change.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-PA-Aug2010-5) The university unveiled a new logo in April 2011. Vice-chancellor Peter John stated that the changes reflected the university's development since 1992 and a new focus on its Brentford and Ealing campuses.

In 2015, a £100 million expansion of the Ealing campus was completed. This work included new facilities such as a new library, student union and updated teaching facilities - building which was highly unpopular with many of the locals.

In 2019 the university merged with [Drama Studio London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_Studio_London "Drama Studio London") in Ealing, and in 2021 it merged with [Ruskin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruskin_College "Ruskin College"), Oxford.

## Campuses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Campuses")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg/250px-TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TVU_Walpole_House_Ealing.jpg)

Walpole House in [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), housing the university's administration.

There are two campus sites in western Greater London, located at St Mary's Road, Ealing and Paragon House in Brentford. There is also a third site in Reading, Berkshire, which is some 35 miles (55 km) from the Ealing sites.

In 2015, the St Mary's Road, Ealing campus underwent a £100 million transformation, with a new social area, library, student union, gym and updated facilities. In 2017, a further £1M was invested in the development of the Paragon campus in Brentford and the addition of a nursing simulation centre in the Reading campus.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Ealing campus is home to The Heathrow Archive, a collection of more than 800 artefacts that tell the story of [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport")'s history from 1946 to 2016.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2017, the University of West London launched its overseas branch campus in [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), United Arab Emirates.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Organisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organisation")]

The University of West London comprises nine schools: The Claude Littner Business School, the London Geller College of Hospitality and Tourism, the School of Computing and Engineering, the London College of Music, the College of Nursing, Midwifery and Healthcare, the School of Law, the School of Human and Social Sciences, the School of Biomedical Sciences, and the London School of Film, Media and Design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-9)

The Graduate School[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-10) (based in Ealing) coordinates and provides support to research activities[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-11) and research degree courses. The University offers traditional PhD programmes and Professional Doctorates.

The university also works with the Met Film School, a private film school that is based at [Ealing Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Studios "Ealing Studios") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-SD-12) The school, which launched in 2003, offers two and three-year bachelor's programmes as well as various master's degree programmes, which are accredited through the University of West London.

In 2020, the university was ranked 34th best university (out of 130+ institutions) in the UK by the 2021 edition of _The Times_ and _Sunday Times_ Good University Guide.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 2021, the university was ranked 34th in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ university guide[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-17) and the university was named the top modern university in London in _[The Guardian University Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian\_University\_Guide "The Guardian University Guide")_ 2022.

The university was ranked 801-1000 in the _Times Higher Education_ Impact Rankings 2024 that evaluates universities worldwide based on their contributions to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). As such, within specific Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), UWL achieved the following rankings: 101-200 for Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10), 301-400 for Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12), and 801-1000 for both Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3) and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG 17).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-18)

The university recorded the best results of any university in Greater London in the annual National Student Survey (NSS) in 2016, with students' responses showing it to be the best University in Greater London for student satisfaction.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-uwl.ac.uk-19) In the NSS 2016, there were 100 per cent overall satisfaction rates for nine courses across the University's eight schools, ranging from Midwifery to Business Studies and Music Technology to Hospitality Management. Among these 100 per cent overall satisfaction rates, the University recorded the best overall satisfaction rates in the UK for Civil Engineering and Building courses in the NSS 2016.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-uwl.ac.uk-19) In 2021, UWL was named the university of the year for student experience in _The Times_ and _Sunday Times_ Good University Guide.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-20)

### Students' Union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Students' Union")]

The University of West London Students' Union (UWLSU) is the recognised student organisation of the University of West London. UWLSU is affiliated with the [National Union of Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Union_of_Students_(United_Kingdom) "National Union of Students (United Kingdom)").

The union has the ground floor of the North Building at the St. Mary's Road campus and is home to a cafe - Coffee Union and social space - Freddie's. The Sports Centre is also located on the Park Road entrance of the St. Mary's Road campus which is open exclusively to UWL staff, students, alumni, and residents that live within the local area. The union also has a space on the second floor at the Paragon campus and a third space on the 9th floor at the Reading campus.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The union aims to bring students academic advice and advocacy support, events, ways to take up new activities, and sports, and a place to socialise. With the course representative programme run by their Student Voice team, students can apply to be a course or school representative to help advocate for academic change.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Student accommodation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Student accommodation")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg/250px-University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_West_London_Building_in_Ealing.jpg)

The University of West London Campus at St Mary's Road, [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing")

Before 2006, the university operated [halls of residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halls_of_residence "Halls of residence") only at the Reading campus, although several private houses in the Ealing area were rented by the university and allocated to students studying there. In September 2006 the university began to offer halls of residence accommodation to students from the Ealing and Slough campuses at a student and keyworker accommodation site named Paragon. The site won the 'Major Housing Project of the Year' category at the 2007 Building Awards, and is in [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford "Brentford"), approximately two miles away from the Ealing campus.

Paragon is home to the tallest building to be completed using [modern methods of construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_methods_of_construction "Modern methods of construction") (MMC) in the UK, which serves as a 130,000 sq ft (12,000 m 2) academic facility for the university's human sciences facility. The student accommodation at Paragon had been criticised by its residents for being too expensive, costing the highest of all Greater London universities' halls of residence along with [SOAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAS "SOAS") in the 2007–2008 year. TVU defended the costs, asserting that the halls are of an especially high standard.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-22)

In 2020, [Notting Hill Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Genesis "Notting Hill Genesis"), the company that owned the Paragon student lets site, controversially closed the entire student halls of residence[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-23) due to fire safety concerns, asking students to immediately evacuate. Students were moved to temporary housing in nearby Wembley whilst the university found suitable housing. Accommodation for students at UWL now varies from shared housing to student lets in Ealing, Acton and the surrounding area.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-24)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_West_London&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In the mid-1990s, its high-profile vice-chancellor, [Mike Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Fitzgerald_(academic) "Mike Fitzgerald (academic)"), ushered through a networked "New Learning Environment" for undergraduate students, involving a shift to online delivery and assessment. The NLE was discontinued in this form, and Fitzgerald resigned in 1998 following a negative [Quality Assurance Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_Assurance_Agency "Quality Assurance Agency") report stating there were "significant management failures" in the delivery of this model.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_West_London#cite_note-25) The University suffered severe financial shortfalls in the years that followed.

The **University of Nottingham** is a public [research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), England. It was founded as **University College Nottingham** in 1881, and was granted a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") as a university in 1948.

Nottingham's main campus ([University Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Park_Campus,_Nottingham "University Park Campus, Nottingham")), the Jubilee Campus and the main teaching hospital ([Queen's Medical Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Medical_Centre "Queen's Medical Centre")) are located within the [City of Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Nottingham "City of Nottingham"), with a number of smaller campuses and sites elsewhere in [Nottinghamshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottinghamshire "Nottinghamshire") and [Derbyshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derbyshire "Derbyshire"). Outside the UK, the university has campuses in [Semenyih, Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semenyih,_Malaysia "Semenyih, Malaysia"), and [Ningbo, China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ningbo,_China "Ningbo, China"). UK academic operations are organised into five faculties, and the university has more than 46,000 students and 7,000 staff across the UK, China and Malaysia. It had an income of £845 million in 2024–25, of which £140.3 million was from research grants and contracts, with an expenditure of £924.2 million.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-Nottingham_Financial_Statement_24/25-1)

The institution's alumni, staff and former staff have won three [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") and a [Fields Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_Medal "Fields Medal"). The university is a member of the [Russell Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group") and the international [Universitas 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universitas_21 "Universitas 21") network.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding")]

The University of Nottingham traces its origins to both the founding of an [adult education school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_school "Normal school") in 1798, and the University Extension Lectures inaugurated by the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") in 1873, which were launched at Nottingham before expanding to other posts of the country.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-ReferenceA-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-13) However, the foundation of the university is generally regarded as being the establishment of University College Nottingham, in 1881 as a college preparing students for examinations of the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London").

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/University_College_Nottingham.jpg/250px-University_College_Nottingham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_College_Nottingham.jpg)

University College Nottingham

In 1875, an anonymous donor provided £10,000 to establish the work of the Adult Education School and Cambridge Extension Lectures on a permanent basis, and the Corporation of Nottingham agreed to erect and maintain a building for this purpose and to provide funds to supply the instruction.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-ReferenceA-12)

The foundation stone of the college was duly laid in 1877 by the former Prime Minister [William Ewart Gladstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ewart_Gladstone "William Ewart Gladstone"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-NottinghamBriefHistory-14) and the college's neo-gothic building on Shakespeare Street was formally opened on 30 July 1881 by [Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Leopold,_Duke_of_Albany "Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany"), with the college admitting its first students that autumn[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-NottinghamBriefHistory-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-jisc-15) In 1881, there were four professors – of Literature, Physics, Chemistry and Natural Science. New departments and chairs quickly followed: Engineering in 1884, Classics combined with Philosophy in 1893, French in 1897 and Education in 1905; in 1905 the combined Department of Physics and Mathematics became two separate entities; in 1911 Departments of English and Mining were created, in 1912, Economics, and Geology combined with Geography; History in 1914, Adult Education in 1923 and Pharmacy in 1925.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) The university college was part of the Borough of Nottingham, under the town clerk's department, until it was incorporated by royal charter in 1903. While this made it formally independent, there was almost complete overlap between the city council and the court of governors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-jisc-15)

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 10: Trent Building](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/0130_-_England%2C_Nottingham%2C_Trent_Building_HDR_-HQ-.jpg/250px-0130_-_England%2C_Nottingham%2C_Trent_Building_HDR_-HQ-.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:0130_-_England,_Nottingham,_Trent_Building_HDR_-HQ-.jpg)

University of Nottingham's Trent Building

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Jesse_Boot_1909.jpg/250px-Jesse_Boot_1909.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jesse_Boot_1909.jpg)

Sir Jesse Boot, pictured, significantly contributed to the development of the university during the 1920s.

Following the first world war, the university college's leadership proposed the creation of a federal East Midlands University, taking in University College Nottingham, [University College Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester"), [Loughborough College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_College "Loughborough College"), and other colleges in Lincoln, Derby and Northampton. A charter was drawn up for the federal university but the proposed dominance of Nottingham led to opposition from Leicester in 1923, and in 1927 the proposal was dropped in favour of Nottingham pursuing university status on its own.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-jisc-15)

The university college underwent significant expansion in the 1920s, when it moved from the centre of Nottingham to a large campus on the city's outskirts. The new campus, called University Park, was completed in 1928, and financed by an endowment fund, public contributions, and the generosity of [Sir Jesse Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Boot "Jesse Boot") (later Lord Trent) who presented 35 acres (14 ha) to the City of Nottingham in 1921.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-16) Boot and his fellow benefactors sought to establish an "elite seat of learning" committed to widening participation,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-17) and hoped that the move would solve the problems facing University College Nottingham, in its restricted building on Shakespeare Street. Boot stipulated that, whilst part of the Highfields site, lying south-west of the city, should be devoted to the university college, the rest should provide a place of recreation for the residents of the city, and, by the end of the decade, the landscaping of the lake and public park adjoining University Boulevard was completed. The original university college building on Shakespeare Street in central Nottingham, known as the Arkwright Building, now forms part of [Nottingham Trent University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham_Trent_University "Nottingham Trent University")'s City Campus.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-18)

University College Nottingham was initially accommodated within the [Trent Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trent_Building "Trent Building"), an imposing white limestone structure with a distinctive clock tower, designed by Morley Horder, and formally opened by [King George V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_George_V "King George V") on 10 July 1928. During this period of development, Nottingham attracted high-profile visiting speakers, including [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein "Albert Einstein"), [H. G. Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells "H. G. Wells"), and [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-19) The blackboard used by Einstein for his lecture at Nottingham is still on display in the Physics department.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-20)

Apart from its physical transfer to surroundings that could not be more different from its original home, the college made few developments between the wars. The Department of Slavonic Languages (later Slavonic Studies) was established in 1933, the teaching of Russian having been introduced in 1916. In 1933–34, the departments of Electrical Engineering, Zoology and Geography, which had been combined with other subjects, were made independent; and in 1938 a supplemental charter provided for a much wider representation on the governing body. However, further advances were delayed by the outbreak of war in 1939.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-ReferenceA-12)

### Second World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Second World War")]

350-400 students from [Goldsmiths' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsmiths,_University_of_London "Goldsmiths, University of London") and 120 students from the [Institute of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Education "UCL Institute of Education") were evacuated from London to Nottingham during the war. Goldsmiths' arrived on Monday 18 September 1939.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-21) At the time it was the largest teacher training college in the country and included the artist [Evelyn Gibbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Gibbs "Evelyn Gibbs") on its staff.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-NEP1945-22) The Institute of Education returned to London in July 1943.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-23) However, the Goldsmiths' buildings in London had been badly damaged so the college remained in Nottingham for another year.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-NEP1945-22)

### University status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: University status")]

Until 1948, students of University College Nottingham students sat exams from and were awarded degrees by the University of London.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-24) In 1948, the institution was granted a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") as the University of Nottingham, giving it university status and the power to confer its own degrees.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-25)

In the 1940s, the Midlands Agricultural and Dairy College at [Sutton Bonington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Bonington "Sutton Bonington") merged with the university as the School of Agriculture, and in 1956 the Portland Building was completed to complement the Trent Building. In 1970, the university established the UK's first new medical school of the 20th century.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-NottinghamBriefHistory-14)

### Modern day

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nottingham&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Modern day")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/University_Park_MMB_%C2%ABB5_Portland_Building.jpg/250px-University_Park_MMB_%C2%ABB5_Portland_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_Park_MMB_%C2%ABB5_Portland_Building.jpg)

University Park, Portland Building

In 1999, Jubilee Campus was opened on the former site of the [Raleigh Bicycle Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh_Bicycle_Company "Raleigh Bicycle Company"), one mile (1.6 km) away from the [University Park Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Park_Campus,_Nottingham "University Park Campus, Nottingham"). Nottingham then began to expand overseas, opening campuses in [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") and in China in 1999 and 2004 respectively. In 2005, the [King's Meadow Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Meadow_Campus "King's Meadow Campus") opened near University Park.

In 2008, the "[Nottingham Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham_Two "Nottingham Two")", a member of staff and a postgraduate student at the university, were detained for under the Terrorism Act 2000 after the university reported finding an edited version of the [al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda") training manual the student was using for his research.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-27) Subsequently, the teaching of terrorism studies was dropped at the university.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-sabir2010-28)

The university's [student rag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rag_(student_society) "Rag (student society)"), Karnival, was suspended in 2016 to ensure compliance with the Charities Act 2016, particularly in the safeguarding of participants in fundraising activities and the people they interacted with.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-29) It was reinstated later that year, but an investigation the following year, 2017, determined that "RAG raids" had breached the safeguarding requirements and health and safety policies on multiple occasions, leading the students' union executive to ban these activities.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-30)

In the 2020–21 academic year, students of the University of Nottingham organised large-scale campaigns for wider academic, welfare, and financial support for students during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-33)

In 2021, the university briefly blocked the appointment of a Catholic chaplain due to his social media posts on [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") and [euthanasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanasia "Euthanasia").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-Anti-abortion_priest_%E2%80%98cancelled%E2%80%99_by_university-35) The university maintained that their concern was not about the priest's views but the way they had been expressed. Following discussions, the priest was able to take up the post the following month.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-36)

In November 2023, the University of Nottingham became the first university in the UK to be awarded an institutional [Athena SWAN Gold Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_SWAN "Athena SWAN") for its commitment to advancing gender equality.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-37)

In January 2025, the university announced plans to sell its King's Meadow Campus.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-King's_Meadow_sale-38) In November 2025, the university announced that it would permanently suspend 16 courses, including all modern language and music courses, for new students,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-39) and that it intended to sell its Castle Meadow Campus.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-Castle_Meadow_sale-40) It cited "significant financial challenges" due to decreasing numbers of students, especially international students, as the reason.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-41) The accounts for 2024/25 revealed that the Castle Meadow Campus, which the university bought for £37.5 million in 2021 and spent over £40 million refurbishing, was now valued at between £14.8 and £18 million.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-Post_2025_accounts-42)

In May 2026, the university announced that it could run out of money within five years if further cuts were not made, and warned 2,700 staff that they were at risk of redundancy. The university said it plans to cut over 600 academic and support posts through voluntary redundancies: over 150 in medicine and health science, 134 in the arts faculty, 108 in social sciences, 97 in sciences, and 38 in engineering.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-44) These cuts amount to over 30% of staff in some departments.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-chemistry-world-cuts-45) Petitions against the cuts at the Chemistry and Physics departments have gained signatures from thousands of academics, including several Nobel Laureates and BBC science presenters.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-chemistry-world-cuts-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-46) Presenter and emeritus professor [Jim Al-Khalili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Al-Khalili "Jim Al-Khalili") stated that "Nottingham Physics is one of the most respected and prestigious departments in the country, and this proposed ‘cull’ would be both devastating and foolish", while Nobel prize-winner [Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Penrose "Roger Penrose") added that "the decision to dismiss this large group of physics and astronomy faculty members at the University of Nottingham, through no fault of their own, is appalling and should be reversed immediately".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-47)

In June 2026, the university informed students and alumni that it had suffered a data breach in its [Campus Solutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PeopleSoft#Post-Oracle_acquisition "PeopleSoft") system, provided by [Oracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation"). Students' personal and financial data was exposed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-49) University management had spent £16.4 million introducing the system.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham#cite_note-50)
